existing.description_long: The Social Security Administration — which serves over 73 million beneficiaries — faced a planned workforce reduction of up to 50 percent, with internal documents confirming plans to cut at least 7,000 of 60,000 employees. DOGE published a list of 47 SSA field offices to be shuttered across the country, concentrated in the South and Southeast, while simultaneously requiring millions of recipients to visit in-person offices rather than conduct business by phone. Acting SSA Commissioner Leland Dudek privately admitted to advocates that 'DOGE people are learning and they will make mistakes, but we have to let them see what is going on.' Former Commissioner Martin O'Malley predicted system collapse within 90 days, warning the loss of experienced IT staff managing SSA's 'fragile and interdependent' computer systems could interrupt benefit payments. By end of 2025, OPM data showed SSA had lost 6,855 net employees.

existing.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia: Wrongly Deported to CECOT, Supreme Court Orders Return
existing.description_short: Kilmar Abrego Garcia: Wrongly Deported to CECOT, Supreme Court Orders Return
existing.description_long: On March 15, 2025, the Trump administration deported Kilmar Armando Abrego Garcia — a Salvadoran man who had legally lived in Maryland for a decade with a work permit and no criminal record — to El Salvador's notorious CECOT mega-prison, in explicit violation of a 2019 immigration court 'withholding order' barring his removal there. The government acknowledged the deportation was an 'administrative error.' District Judge Paula Xinis ordered his return by April 7; the Supreme Court unanimously upheld the order on April 10 (Noem v. Abrego Garcia), requiring the government to 'facilitate' his return. Despite the Supreme Court ruling, the Trump administration for months refused to take meaningful steps to secure his release from CECOT, with officials arguing U.S. courts lacked jurisdiction once he crossed the border — a position Justice Sotomayor called an argument for unchecked power to deport even U.S. citizens.

existing.title: OMB Spending Freeze Attempts to Seize Congress Power of the Purse
existing.description_short: OMB Spending Freeze Attempts to Seize Congress Power of the Purse
existing.description_long: On January 27, 2025, the Office of Management and Budget issued a sweeping directive ordering federal agencies to pause billions of dollars in congressionally approved grants and loans — including funding for healthcare, housing assistance, and disaster relief — pending a review for alignment with Trump's executive orders. The move was described by legal experts as an attempted assertion of an unconstitutional impoundment power not seen since Richard Nixon. The Constitution's Article I explicitly vests the power of the purse in Congress. A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order within 24 hours. OMB Director Russell Vought publicly stated in June 2025 that impoundment was certainly not off the table. The administration's sustained effort to cancel, freeze, and redirect congressionally appropriated funds throughout 2025 generated dozens of lawsuits; courts largely blocked the moves but the legal battle was ongoing as of August 2026.

existing.title: $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee Proclamation Triggers Mass Panic Among Tech Workers
existing.description_short: $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee Proclamation Triggers Mass Panic Among Tech Workers
existing.description_long: On September 19, 2025, Trump signed a proclamation imposing a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions — the program used to hire approximately 500,000 skilled foreign workers annually, primarily in tech, healthcare, and research. The ambiguous rollout left hundreds of thousands of existing H-1B holders abroad scrambling to return before a Sunday deadline, fearing they would be locked out of the U.S. without paying $100,000. Microsoft, Amazon, Goldman Sachs and other major employers sent emergency memos; workers abandoned family visits and canceled trips. The White House clarified on Saturday — after 24 hours of chaos — that the fee applied only to new petitions, not renewals or existing holders abroad. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had incorrectly said it was an annual fee; the White House then said it was one-time. Economists projected the policy would accelerate offshoring and shrink the U.S. labor force.

original_title: 4,240 Trans Troops Identified for Forced Discharge

existing.title: 4,240 Trans Troops Identified for Forced Discharge
existing.description_short: 4,240 Trans Troops Identified for Forced Discharge
existing.description_long: A February 26, 2025 Defense Department memo announced that military personnel diagnosed with gender dysphoria would be discharged, setting a June 6, 2025 deadline for voluntary separation with financial bonuses for active-duty members, and July 7 for National Guard and Reserve. The Pentagon identified 4,240 service members — approximately 0.2 percent of the 2.1 million in uniform — with a gender dysphoria diagnosis as of December 9, 2024, far below the previous estimate of 15,000 transgender troops. By early May 2025, roughly 1,000 had voluntarily come forward to separate, about a quarter of those identified; the Army alone accounted for approximately 500. After June 6, involuntary separations began for those who had not self-identified. Defense records showed the military had spent approximately $15 million over five years on gender-affirming care for these service members, a fraction of the $300 million spent on erectile dysfunction medications in a comparable period.

existing.description_short: Trump Refuses to Comply With SCOTUS Abrego Garcia Order — Unprecedented Defiance
existing.description_long: Following the Supreme Court's April 10, 2025 order directing the Trump administration to facilitate the return of wrongly deported Kilmar Abrego Garcia from El Salvador's CECOT prison, the Trump administration refused to take meaningful steps to comply. Senior officials including White House aide Stephen Miller publicly stated the administration would not bring Abrego Garcia back, arguing the Court's order to 'facilitate' return did not require actually securing his release. The administration claimed El Salvador, whose authoritarian president Nayib Bukele had taken a personal call with Trump celebrating the deportations, had exclusive custody and the U.S. had no power to compel his release — despite having engineered his transfer there in the first place. Legal scholars and opposition lawmakers described the defiance as the most serious constitutional crisis since Watergate, representing a direct rejection of Supreme Court authority. Multiple federal judges held proceedings to compel compliance; the administration continued stonewalling.
